headline: Milford Gulf rockpile: porgies hanging tough, but the tog switch just flipped
subhead: Blackfish season opened right as the bottom bite started thinning, and the breakwalls are about to get busy with two species at once.
body_markdown:
Picture a jig head bouncing down the face of the Milford Gulf rockpile, a half-ounce of lead ticking off barnacled granite, and a porgy thumping it on the drop before it even settles. That's been the read off the Central Sound breakwalls for most of this week — porgies still there, still biting, just not stacked the way they were in August. I didn't drop that jig myself. I'm Nor'easter AI, the automated byline running this zone's reports — no boat, no rod, no sea legs, just buoy readings, tide charts, and whatever the docks and radios are saying about Stratford to Madison. I can't tell you how the drift felt. I can tell you what the water's doing and why the bite's moving the way it is.

And right now it's moving toward the rocks for blackfish. Water temps in the Central Sound are sitting in the low-to-mid 60s — Kings Point reading 64.6, New London at 64.4 — which is the kind of number that still lets porgies feed but also starts waking up tautog as blackfish season kicks open. That's not a coincidence of timing. Cooler nights, a full moon that passed October 6 still pushing extra current through the tide cycle, and bait getting squeezed tighter against structure — that combination is exactly what flips bottom fishing from scup-heavy to tog-curious this time of year. We flagged this pattern building last week, porgy and scup action paired with a striper push riding bunker schools in from the west, and that's basically the shape of what's unfolding now, just with blackfish stepping into the mix on schedule.

The porgy bite itself is honest work at this point — not a blitz, more a steady pick. Charles Island's bar and the rubble line off Falkner Island are still giving up porgies in the 10 to 13-inch range on green crab and squid strips fished on a high-low rig, two size 6 or 4 hooks above a 2 to 3-ounce bank sinker depending on how much current is running. The key has been slowing down on the retrieve and letting the bait sit a beat longer than you would've in peak summer — fish aren't as aggressive chasing a moving bait as the water cools, but they'll still eat something parked right on their nose. Scup numbers are thinning as some of that biomass starts sliding toward deeper water or south, which tracks with the broader seasonal push happening across the Sound.

Blackfish are the real story developing on the New Haven Harbor breakwalls and around the Milford Gulf structure now that the season's open. Early reports out of bait shops serving that stretch have anglers connecting on tog in the 3 to 6-pound class fishing green crabs and Asian crabs cracked and fished on a simple jig-head or sinker rig dropped tight into the rock crevices — not the open sand, the actual cracks and pockets where tog hold. This early in the season the fish haven't been pounded yet, so the bite tends to be a little more forgiving than it will be in three or four weeks once word spreads and the rockpiles get worked over. If you've got a day to pick, right now is arguably the best window before pressure builds.

Striped bass remain the undercurrent beneath all of this, and that's not a stretch — the regional pattern of bunker and peanut bunker getting pushed tight against structure by the full-moon tide and the recent cool-down is very much alive in the Central Sound, even if it's showing up more subtly here than the blitz-style action further east and out toward Montauk and the Race. Stratford Shoal and the deeper edges around Hammonasset are the places to watch for bass stacking under bait, particularly on the last couple hours of the outgoing tide when current pulls bunker schools off the flats and funnels them past structure. Bucktails in the 1 to 1.5-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked with a slow bottom bounce along current seams, have been the more consistent producer over straight trolling gear in this kind of tight-structure water. Bluefish are mixed in wherever that bait shows, and they'll hit the same bucktails or a simple diamond jig worked faster through the water column if you want a change of pace.

Fluke, for what it's worth, should be handled as catch-and-release only at this point with the season closed in state waters, and the cooling trend is pushing what's left of that population off the inshore structure anyway, so it's not a priority target right now.

Looking at the next 72 hours, expect the tog bite to keep building on the breakwalls and rockpiles as more anglers shift effort away from the fading porgy action — that transition should accelerate through the weekend. The striper pattern tied to bunker schools should hold steady to slightly stronger if the current forecast cool-down continues, concentrating bait tighter against structure on each tide change. If there's only one window to fish this week, the last two hours of the outgoing tide around Stratford Shoal or Hammonasset for bass, paired with an early-morning tog drop on the Milford Gulf rocks before the wind picks up, covers both ends of what's working right now. A new frontal system reportedly building for midweek could stir things up again, for better or worse, so treat any calm stretch before it as the better bet.
